topics.title: Sovereign data spaces
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not a claim of deployed availability.
topics.summary: Policy-scoped spaces retain local authority, visibility, admission, privacy, and validator boundaries while approved value and evidence can coordinate across one logical ledger.

topics.title: Cross-data-space atomic transactions
topics.claim_scope: Published-page paraphrase. Diagram topology is an observed transcription of the supplied screenshot, not independent protocol specification.
topics.summary: An AMX transaction declares participating spaces and read/write sets. Each space prepares against a common snapshot; Nexus commits only when every required result is valid, otherwise it aborts without partial effects.

diagram.caption: Two data spaces prepare independently; a 2-of-2 Nexus latch allows atomic delivery and payment or restores both roots.
diagram.text_equivalent: Data space A stages A0 to A1 and returns Prepare QC A. Data space B stages B0 to B1 and returns Prepare QC B. The Nexus latch shows 2/2 prepared. Payment A to B and delivery B to A lock together. All valid evidence commits both; any failed proof or policy restores both roots.

topics.title: Hyperledger Iroha 3 Core
topics.claim_scope: SORA-page description; code provenance is provided separately in the repository registry.
topics.summary: SORA Nexus describes Iroha 3 as its deterministic execution core: Torii admits traffic, Kotodama compiles high-level programs, IVM executes bounded logic, and Sumeragi/Kura preserve canonical history.

topics.title: Sumeragi consensus
topics.claim_scope: SORA-page paraphrase; not an independent implementation audit.
topics.summary: Prepare and Commit quorum certificates bind finality to an exact block subject and frozen validator context; portable commit evidence can be independently checked against trusted context.

topics.title: A shared economy for AI agents
topics.claim_scope: The SORA page calls this a future use case. It is not a product availability, autonomy, wallet, payment, or integration claim.
topics.summary: The page presents future machine-to-machine exchange using accounts, assets, permissions, automation, atomic delivery, receipts, and human-defined authority. It explicitly says Iroha does not run AI models or grant unrestricted autonomy.

topics.title: ISO 20022 Gateway
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an integration, deployment or regulatory-approval claim.
topics.summary: The page describes a path in which pacs.008 and pacs.009 payment messages are validated at Torii, mapped to ledger-native instructions, and answered with a deterministic pacs.002 status.

topics.title: Deterministic settlement router
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not a live pricing, reserve or settlement-service claim.
topics.summary: The page presents deterministic quantity conversion, margins, haircuts and lane-specific buffer policy, with lane commitments, receipts and telemetry for reconciliation.

topics.title: Lanes + Merge Ledger
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an independent performance benchmark.
topics.summary: Independent workloads execute in parallel lanes and their certified commitments converge into one canonical merge-ledger history.

topics.title: Runtime lane lifecycle
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an instruction to alter network topology.
topics.summary: The page describes authorized, signed lifecycle changes that add, replace or retire capacity through a committed lane catalogue and safety gates.

topics.title: Verifiable finality proofs
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; trusted chain context remains an external verifier responsibility.
topics.summary: A portable finality proof combines a canonical header, execution commitment, Commit QC, frozen roster and proofs of possession, then binds to independently trusted chain context.

topics.title: Kotodama Programs
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an executable-programming interface.
topics.summary: The page describes readable Kotodama programs compiling to bounded IVM bytecode so validators use the same deterministic runtime.

topics.title: Iroha Special Instructions
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it never authorizes any ledger operation.
topics.summary: Typed native instructions cover asset definitions, minting, transfer, permissions and supply changes; ordered batches stage dependent changes as one result or discard them together.

topics.title: Capability manifests
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an access grant or policy decision.
topics.summary: The page describes data-space authority scoped by program, method, asset and role, with activation, expiry, amount limits, allowance windows and deny-wins rules.

topics.title: On-Chain Automation
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; no automated action can be triggered by this corpus.
topics.summary: A registered trigger holds one executable, event filter, authority and repeat policy; permissions and bounded runtime controls constrain execution and record its outcome.

topics.title: Norito Codec
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an independent codec conformance test.
topics.summary: Typed values are encoded in schema-bound frames with version, schema hash, compression, length, integrity checksum and layout metadata for exact validation and reconstruction.

topics.title: SoraNet + SoraFS
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it does not make a storage, relay, payment or availability guarantee.
topics.summary: The page presents a blinded relay path and content-addressed retrieval in which manifests bind chunks, order, length and digests before verified reconstruction.

topics.title: FASTPQ Proof Pipeline
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not a privacy or compliance certification.
topics.summary: The page describes private execution commitments becoming proof inputs so public admission can verify required evidence without receiving the complete private trace.

topics.title: Privacy-proof admission
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not a proof-verification service.
topics.summary: Lane manifests register commitments or proof descriptors; admission checks a supplied witness against the routed lane registry and fails closed if accepted evidence is absent.

topics.title: Data Availability & Proofs
topics.claim_scope: Paraphrase of the cited SORA page; it is not an availability SLA or retrieval guarantee.
topics.summary: The page presents recoverable committed history through sharding, sampling and reconstruction so proofs remain connected to retrievable data.

atlas.title: ISO 20022 Gateway
explanation: pacs.008 and pacs.009 institutional payment messages enter through Torii.
Schema and policy validation map accepted messages to Iroha-native instructions and return deterministic pacs.002 status.
sequence: Receive pacs.008 or pacs.009.
Validate schema and policy.
Execute the mapped Iroha instruction.
Return accepted, rejected or settled pacs.002 status.

diagram.caption: Institutional message ingress becomes deterministic ledger action and canonical status.

atlas.title: Sovereign Data Spaces
explanation: Each space retains policy, visibility, admission, privacy and validator boundaries.
Only authorised value and evidence cross a boundary; the full private state does not.
sequence: Apply local policy in public or restricted space.
Receive an explicitly authorised boundary request.
Coordinate approved evidence and value across the shared logical ledger.

diagram.caption: Separate public and restricted spaces operate under local policy while authorised flows cross an explicit boundary.

atlas.title: Cross-data-space atomic transactions
explanation: An AMX transaction declares spaces and read/write sets against one authority snapshot.
All participants prepare and provide valid evidence before both state transitions commit; any failure restores both roots.
sequence: Declare spaces, read/write sets and snapshot.
Stage A0→A1 and B0→B1; obtain participant prepare QCs.
Expose a 2-of-2 prepared latch.
Move payment and delivery under one atomic lock.
Commit both legs with a receipt or roll both back.

diagram.caption: Two spaces prepare independently and pass a 2-of-2 Nexus latch before atomic commit or rollback.

atlas.title: Deterministic settlement router
explanation: Exact quantity conversion, oracle input, margins, haircuts and lane-buffer policy produce a replayable settlement result.
Lane commitments, receipts and telemetry support operator and auditor reconciliation.
sequence: Validate amount, oracle, margin and liquidity policy.
Calculate canonical XOR obligation and applied haircut.
Check lane buffer state.
Seal lane commitment and emit reconciliation receipt.

diagram.caption: One obligation passes canonical input, conversion, haircut, buffer policy and lane commitment.

atlas.title: Hyperledger Iroha 3 Core
explanation: Torii admits traffic, Kotodama compiles high-level programs and IVM runs bounded deterministic logic.
Lane routing provides capacity while Sumeragi finality and Kura preserve a single canonical history.
sequence: Torii admits a signed request.
Kotodama compiles it for IVM execution.
The runtime routes it through an assigned lane.
Sumeragi and Kura seal canonical commit.

diagram.caption: Admission, compilation, deterministic execution, routing and canonical commit run as one core.

atlas.title: Lanes + Merge Ledger
explanation: Independent workloads execute in parallel rather than one queue.
Certified lane commitments converge into one merge-ledger history rather than separate chains.
sequence: Route independent workloads into parallel lanes.
Produce certified commitment per lane.
Order commitments into one merge-ledger block.

diagram.caption: Parallel lanes converge into a shared history.

atlas.title: Runtime lane lifecycle
explanation: Authorised signed lifecycle changes commit to exact lane catalogues and incarnations.
Stale catalogues, invalid plans and unsafe retirement are rejected; routing, storage and telemetry reconcile after commit.
sequence: Review catalogue and sign lifecycle plan.
Validate authority, commitment, incarnation and safety gates.
Commit topology update and refresh routing.
Bring lane online or retire only after outstanding work clears.

diagram.caption: A signed plan validates, adds, routes, drains and retires capacity under consensus.

atlas.title: Sumeragi Consensus
explanation: Prepare and Commit quorum certificates bind an exact subject, frozen validator roster, height and deterministic transition.
Bodies, vote intent, locks and decisions cross durable storage boundaries before the protocol advances.
sequence: Leader broadcasts signed proposal and manifest.
Validators reconstruct, validate and durably store exact body.
Form Prepare QC from thresholds.
Persist lock and release Commit votes.
Persist Commit QC decision, apply body and open next height.

diagram.caption: Deterministic BFT finality advances through proposal, durable validation, prepare QC, lock and commit QC.

atlas.title: Verifiable finality proofs
explanation: A portable proof includes canonical header, certified subject, execution roots, Commit QC, frozen roster and proofs of possession.
A verifier binds the proof to independently trusted context and checks structure, signer membership, dual quorum and aggregate BLS signature.
sequence: Assemble header, subject, roots, QC, roster and PoPs.
Seal Norito proof envelope.
Bind to trusted chain/context anchor.
Verify bindings, quorums, signer order, PoPs and aggregate signature.

diagram.caption: Exact finality evidence is sealed then checked against an external trusted anchor.

atlas.title: Kotodama Programs
explanation: Readable Kotodama source compiles to bounded IVM bytecode.
Every validator executes the same bounded runtime and derives the same state transition.
sequence: Write readable Kotodama source.
Compile to IVM bytecode.
Consume bounded cycle budget.
Derive identical state transition on every validator.

diagram.caption: Source compiles into bounded bytecode for deterministic peer execution.

atlas.title: Iroha Special Instructions
explanation: Native typed operations cover definitions, mint, transfer, permissions and burn under explicit authority.
An ordered batch stages dependent changes and commits all or discards all on failure.
sequence: Register asset definition with supply zero.
Mint after authority and policy checks.
Transfer without changing supply.
Grant permission.
Burn and commit final state.

diagram.caption: An ordered ISI batch stages native state transitions then commits one result.

atlas.title: Capability manifests
explanation: A manifest scopes a universal account’s authority by data space, program, method, asset and optional AMX role.
Activation/expiry, amount limits, allowance windows and deny-wins evaluation make authority inspectable and bounded.
sequence: Resolve subject to universal account and active manifest.
Check requested scope and epoch/amount limits.
Scan matching deny rules.
Return allowed grant metadata or structured denial.

diagram.caption: A request resolves context, matches an active manifest, checks denies and returns a verdict.

atlas.title: On-Chain Automation
explanation: A trigger stores one executable, one event filter, declared authority and repeat policy.
Permissions, repeat limits, fuel/cycles, gas and execution depth bound the resulting action and its recorded outcome.
sequence: Register one supported filter configuration.
Matching event loads executable, authority and remaining repeats.
Resolve filter, enabled state, authority and runtime bounds.
Stage state change and consume repeat on success.
Record TriggerCompleted outcome.

diagram.caption: One exact event filter activates bounded authorised work and a completion record.

atlas.title: Norito Codec
explanation: Typed values use canonical payloads framed by an NRT0 header with version, schema hash, compression, declared length, CRC64-XZ and layout flags.
Readers validate boundaries before reconstruction; uncompressed canonical layout produces the same bytes for the same value.
sequence: Serialize ordered fields.
Seal 40-byte NRT0 header.
Stream header and payload.
Validate magic, version, layout, schema, length and CRC.
Decode the same typed value.

diagram.caption: A typed value becomes a checked frame and reconstructs exactly.

atlas.title: SoraNet + SoraFS
explanation: A blinded request selects entry, middle and exit relay roles under strict transport policy.
SoraFS resolves a manifest, retrieves chunks from eligible providers and validates chunks and completed payload before returning evidence.
sequence: Turn content address into blinded key.
Select SoraNet path by role/version/policy.
Cross entry, middle and exit relays.
Resolve SoraFS manifest and expected digests.
Retrieve ordered provider chunks and verify reconstruction.
Return verified object and fetch evidence.

diagram.caption: A blinded relay request resolves manifest-bound chunks then returns verified content.

atlas.title: A shared economy for AI agents
explanation: The page presents a future use case using accounts, assets, permissions, automation, atomic delivery and receipts under human-defined authority.
It explicitly says Iroha does not run AI models, determine AI control, or grant unrestricted autonomy.
sequence: Buyer requests a machine-readable service.
Check authority, balance and spending limits.
Provider registers or mints service asset.
Enter payment and delivery in atomic transaction.
Commit both sides or roll both back.
Emit canonical audit receipt.

diagram.caption: Authorised accounts exchange payment and digital rights atomically under human policy.

atlas.title: FASTPQ Proof Pipeline
explanation: Private execution traces remain within their data space while commitments become public proof inputs.
A public verifier reaches admission without receiving the complete trace; privacy does not remove correctness checks.
sequence: Keep private execution trace within its data space.
Create public commitment and proof inputs.
Verify evidence and decide admission without exposing trace.

diagram.caption: Private trace produces a public commitment and a verified admission decision.

atlas.title: Privacy-proof admission
explanation: Lane manifests register approved commitments such as Merkle roots or proof descriptors.
Transactions attach a witness; admission checks it against the routed lane registry and fails closed when required evidence is absent, malformed or unregistered.
sequence: Governance registers commitment identifiers and verification parameters.
Transaction attaches witness for routed lane.
Admission verifies attachment and applies lane-compliance rule.
Accept valid evidence or reject before queueing.

diagram.caption: A private-data-space witness is checked against a lane proof policy before admission.

atlas.title: Data Availability & Proofs
explanation: Committed history is made recoverable through sharding, sampling and reconstruction.
Availability evidence keeps proofs connected to data that can be retrieved rather than only an opaque commitment.
sequence: Commit data into availability structure.
Shard data for distribution.
Sample and verify availability evidence.
Recover/reconstruct committed history when required.

diagram.caption: Committed data is sharded, sampled and reconstructed to keep proofs tied to retrievable history.

whitepaper.title: Hyperledger Iroha 3: SORA Nexus
whitepaper.notice: This JSON represents the paper by page-anchored sections and detailed summaries. It does not replace, amend, or reproduce the canonical PDF wording.
whitepaper.claim_scope: Document representation only; not an implementation specification, deployment claim, operational interface, legal commitment, or performance guarantee.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.summary: Introduces SORA Nexus as a single logical ledger built on Hyperledger Iroha 3. The stated design combines cooperating validators and data spaces to support privacy, deterministic execution, and interoperability across regulated and open domains.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.summary: Sets out the paper’s first-principles case for a unified ledger architecture rather than separate public and private chains. It frames data sovereignty, deterministic execution, cryptographic proofs, availability, and institutional interoperability as one system design.

sections.title: SORA Nexus Highlights
sections.summary: Summarises the stated architecture: data spaces, lanes and a merge ledger, the Iroha Virtual Machine and Kotodama, Sumeragi finality, FASTPQ proofs, data availability, ISO 20022 alignment, and Norito serialization.

sections.title: SORA Nexus: The End of History
sections.summary: Presents the paper’s unification thesis: financial and digital systems should be able to coordinate on one logical ledger without forcing every participant into the same visibility, policy, or validator regime.

sections.title: Context and Goals
sections.summary: Defines the architectural motivation: public chains can expose data and make performance difficult to predict, while isolated systems lose composability. The intended goal is common settlement with bounded policy and privacy domains.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.summary: Explains why institutional systems, open applications, and sovereign monetary environments require shared coordination without collapsing their respective governance and information boundaries.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.summary: Organises the desired properties around deterministic operation, privacy, interoperability, scalable capacity, auditable governance, and common history across differentiated data spaces.

sections.title: IVM at the Core
sections.summary: Places the Iroha Virtual Machine at the execution core. The paper describes a controlled deterministic runtime intended to make high-level programs and native instructions resolve consistently across peers.

sections.title: Architecture Overview
sections.summary: Introduces the major architectural components and their roles: data spaces for bounded domains, lanes for parallel work, a merge ledger for canonical ordering, and shared execution and finality machinery.

sections.title: Components and Roles
sections.summary: Describes how admission, execution, routing, storage, consensus, proof systems, and governance components cooperate while retaining distinct responsibilities.

sections.title: Data Spaces
sections.summary: Explains policy-scoped spaces as domains that retain local visibility, admission, privacy, governance, and validator boundaries while authorized evidence and value can coordinate through shared settlement.

sections.title: Lanes and Merge Ledger
sections.summary: Describes parallel execution lanes whose certified commitments converge into a shared canonical history, aiming to add capacity without fragmenting assets, liquidity, or institutional context.

sections.title: Data Space Model and Governance
sections.summary: Covers public and restricted domains and the governance surfaces that define their policies. The stated model treats policy and privacy boundaries as part of the ledger topology rather than after-the-fact application conventions.

sections.title: Consensus, Scheduling, and Finality
sections.summary: Groups the mechanisms for admission, fair scheduling, lane topology changes, and Byzantine finality. The focus is on making the route from request to durable canonical state explicit and reviewable.

sections.title: Data Availability and Storage
sections.summary: Describes erasure-coded storage, availability sampling, certificates, and proof systems intended to keep commitments connected to recoverable data while limiting unnecessary disclosure.

sections.title: Cryptography and Serialization
sections.summary: Covers canonical cryptographic primitives and serialization. Norito is presented as the encoding layer that allows nodes and external systems to validate and reconstruct typed values consistently.

sections.title: Smart Contracts and Execution
sections.summary: Covers Kotodama compilation to IVM bytecode, the rationale for a custom deterministic virtual machine, and runtime interfaces such as ABI, memory, syscalls, and gas boundaries.

sections.title: Transaction Lifecycle and Networking
sections.summary: Describes the path by which signed requests are admitted, propagated, validated, executed, and committed, with the aim that identical inputs and authority context lead to the same network result.

sections.title: Account Model, Encoding, and Multisig
sections.summary: Covers account structure and lifecycle, state application, automation triggers, and multi-signature or authority-related concerns in the wider execution model.

sections.title: Interoperability and Connectors
sections.summary: Addresses connection to institutional and external systems. The paper associates this layer with ISO 20022-aligned messaging, canonical envelopes, and explicit policy boundaries for coordinated value exchange.

sections.title: Ecosystem Components
sections.summary: Indexes SoraFS, SoraNet, Soracles, ISO 20022 alignment, Norito streaming, Kaigi, and Taikai as components around the core ledger and execution architecture.

sections.title: Governance: SORA Parliament
sections.summary: Covers governance bodies and selection, runtime upgrades, the economic model and XOR utility, offline transactions, and developer experience. It frames changes to shared infrastructure as governed and auditable rather than ad hoc.

sections.title: Privacy, Security, and Compliance
sections.summary: Covers privacy transactions, proof systems, and related compliance concerns. Its architectural focus is the verification of narrow claims without treating complete transaction visibility as the default condition.

sections.title: Operations and Observability
sections.summary: Addresses operating and observing the network, including the information needed to understand state, capacity, and execution without conflating observability with unrestricted disclosure.

sections.title: Performance Targets and Defaults
sections.summary: Lists performance-related targets and defaults as part of the document’s design discussion. These are document statements, not independent benchmarks or production service-level commitments in this corpus.

sections.title: Mathematical Foundations
sections.summary: Collects the formal and quantitative material behind start-time fair queuing, lane and data-availability budgets, erasure coding, availability confidence, proof composition, Fiat–Shamir, and XOR fee equilibrium.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.summary: Places the architecture in practical contexts where sovereign policy, shared settlement, privacy boundaries, programmable execution, and interoperability may need to coexist.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Returns to the paper’s central proposition: a shared logical ledger can support differentiated policy and privacy domains when execution, finality, proofs, and governance are designed as mutually bounded components.

case_for_xor.title: The Case for XOR
case_for_xor.author: Makoto Takemiya
case_for_xor.notice: This JSON represents a historical editorial document by page-anchored sections and summaries. It does not replace, amend, or reproduce the canonical PDF wording, and it is not presented as current SORA Nexus policy.
case_for_xor.claim_scope: Historical economic argument only; not financial advice, a token recommendation, legal advice, a legal-tender proposal, an implementation plan, or a present-tense performance or availability statement.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.summary: States the author’s thesis that XOR is a supranational currency whose supply and primary market are managed by a blockchain program. It argues that productive investment and open governance can connect monetary issuance to the creation of goods and services.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces money as a unit of account, store of value, and medium of exchange, then frames the paper as an argument about how a cryptocurrency might be used to support predictable economic growth. It sets up a comparison with Bitcoin’s legal-tender status in El Salvador.

sections.title: Creating Economic Growth
sections.summary: Presents the paper’s account of economic growth through factor inputs and productivity. It distinguishes money used for transactions contributing to GDP from money used for asset purchases, and argues that allocation and use of money affect growth, prices, and asset bubbles.

sections.title: XOR as a Catalyst for Economic Growth
sections.summary: Sets out the paper’s claims about XOR’s bonding-curve model, elastic supply, governance, and intended role in funding productive activity. The paper discusses buy and sell functions, reserves, token voting, and TBCD in support of that argument.

sections.title: Comparison to Bitcoin Legal Tender Status in El Salvador
sections.summary: Compares the paper’s model of XOR with Bitcoin’s legal-tender adoption in El Salvador, discussing remittances, access, distribution infrastructure, currency issuance, mining, and the author’s assessment of economic consequences. These are attributed historical arguments, not current analysis by this corpus.

sections.title: Steps to Implement the SORA Economic System in a Country
sections.summary: Describes the document’s proposed sequence of legislation, wallet localization, liaison and economic-analysis arrangements. This section is retained as historical source material only and is not operational guidance or a current proposal.

sections.title: References
sections.summary: Lists the academic, institutional, technical, and web references cited by the author in support of the paper’s economic and technical arguments.
